title: People value local influence more strongly than they feel able to exercise it
source_unit: UK Department for Culture, Media and Sport / Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, Community and Engagement Survey 2025/26: Influencing Local Decisions

observations.period: 2025/26 Community and Engagement Survey; perceived local influence, importance, and desired involvement

denominator.unit: over 175,000 Community and Engagement Survey responses; people aged 16+ in England

feel_can_influence.unit: percent agreeing definitely or tending to agree that they can personally influence decisions affecting their local area

feel_influence_important.unit: percent saying it is very or quite important to personally influence decisions affecting their local area

want_more_council_involvement.unit: percent wanting greater involvement in decisions made by their local council

importance_efficacy_gap.unit: percentage-point difference between saying influence is important and saying they can influence

mechanism.value: Local legitimacy contains a conversion gap: people can value influence without perceiving usable access, and a smaller but meaningful group wants more involvement beyond current participation

observations.method: Official Community and Engagement Survey estimates for people aged 16+ in England; measures cover perceived personal influence, importance of influence, and desired council involvement.
observations.uncertainty: The measures are self-reported perceptions and aspirations, not observed council responsiveness, decision outcomes, or causal effects; estimates are rounded and the survey uses different question universes where specified.
observations.subgroup: People aged 16+ in England; national estimates for influence, importance, and desired involvement.
observations.counterinterpretation: People may value influence as a democratic principle without wanting frequent participation, while low perceived influence may reflect realistic expectations rather than institutional failure.

observations.period: 2025/26 Community and Engagement Survey; perceived influence by disability and socioeconomic classification

denominator.unit: over 175,000 survey responses; subgroup estimates for people aged 16+ in England

influence_non_disabled.unit: percent of non-disabled people agreeing they can personally influence local decisions

influence_disabled.unit: percent of disabled people agreeing they can personally influence local decisions

influence_higher_professional.unit: percent in higher managerial, administrative, or professional occupations agreeing they can personally influence local decisions

influence_routine_manual.unit: percent in routine and manual occupations agreeing they can personally influence local decisions

influence_never_worked_long_term_unemplo.unit: percent in the never-worked or long-term-unemployed classification agreeing they can personally influence local decisions

mechanism.value: Perceived efficacy does not map cleanly onto occupational status: disability and routine/manual status show lower perceived influence, while the never-worked/long-term-unemployed group reports higher perceived influence than intermediate and routine/manual groups

observations.method: Official subgroup estimates from the Community and Engagement Survey; disability and demographic questions are voluntary and self-reported, and socioeconomic classification is based on occupation and employment status.
observations.uncertainty: Subgroup differences are descriptive and may reflect age, ethnicity, local context, political interest, survey response, service contact, or measurement interpretation; they do not establish individual or institutional causes.
observations.subgroup: People aged 16+ in England by disability status and socioeconomic classification.
observations.counterinterpretation: A higher reported sense of influence in one labor-market group may reflect different expectations, issue exposure, or local political networks rather than greater actual decision power.

observations.period: 2025/26 Community and Engagement Survey; local decision routes and practical access conditions

denominator.unit: over 175,000 survey responses; people aged 16+ in England

most_common_influence_route_petition.unit: percent selecting signing an online petition as a way they would go about influencing local decisions

most_common_influence_route_council.unit: percent selecting contacting the local council or council official

most_common_influence_route_councillor.unit: percent selecting contacting the local councillor

easier_if_know_issues.unit: percent saying knowing what issues were being considered would make influence easier

easier_if_online_email.unit: percent saying the ability to give an opinion online or by email would make influence easier

mechanism.value: People identify low-friction information and digital-contact interfaces as practical access conditions, suggesting that civic voice depends on discoverability and response channels as well as motivation

observations.method: Official Community and Engagement Survey estimates on preferred routes to influence and conditions that would make local influence easier.
observations.uncertainty: These are stated routes and enabling conditions, not observed use, completion, response, or influence; multiple answers may be selected and the source does not identify which channels work for which local issues.
observations.subgroup: People aged 16+ in England; route and access-condition responses.
observations.counterinterpretation: Petitions and digital contact can be low-cost expressions that do not lead to deliberation or institutional change; knowing an issue is being considered may increase awareness without increasing power.

Official technical report for sampling, fieldwork, survey pathways, and interpretation.

boundary: This record adds a perceived-efficacy and practical-access layer between civic participation and institutional legitimacy. It does not measure council response, decision change, policy influence, deliberative quality, or durable trust; estimates are self-reported, descriptive, and subject to the survey's pathway and local-estimate caveats.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official GOV.UK local-decisions report reviewed for headline perceived influence, importance, desired involvement, subgroup, local-authority, route, and practical-access estimates, including rounding and self-report caveats.
